title: What is the difference between `git merge` and `git rebase` for integrating a branch (merge commit preserving history vs replaying commits for a linear history), and what do `stash` and `cherry-pick` do?
shortTitle: `git merge` vs `git rebase`, and what `stash` and `cherry-pick` do

s1_definition.profdef: `git merge` integrates one branch into another by creating a new merge commit that has two parents, preserving the true, branching history exactly as it happened. `git rebase` integrates by replaying your branch's commits one at a time onto the tip of the target branch, producing new commits and a clean linear history. `git stash` temporarily shelves your uncommitted working-directory and staged changes so your working tree is clean, to be reapplied later. `git cherry-pick` copies one specific commit from anywhere and applies it as a new commit on your current branch.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of two ways to combine two sets of ledger corrections at National Bank of India. Merge is like stapling both sets together with a cover note saying "these two streams were combined on this date" — the history honestly shows two parallel efforts joining. Rebase is like rewriting your corrections as if you had started from the other set all along, so everything reads as one straight sequence with no cover note. Stash is like sweeping your half-finished draft forms into a labeled tray so your desk is instantly clear for an urgent task, then pulling them back out later. Cherry-pick is like spotting one specific correction in another officer's batch and copying just that single correction into your own batch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Merge joins histories with a merge commit; rebase replays commits for a linear history; stash shelves uncommitted work; cherry-pick copies one specific commit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `git merge` integrates one branch into another by creating a new merge commit that has two parents, preserving the true, branching history exactly as it happened. `git rebase` integrates by replaying your branch's commits one at a time onto the tip of the target branch, producing new commits and a clean linear history. `git stash` temporarily shelves your uncommitted working-directory and staged changes so your working tree is clean, to be reapplied later. `git cherry-pick` copies one specific commit from anywhere and applies it as a new commit on your current branch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of two ways to combine two sets of ledger corrections at National Bank of India. Merge is like stapling both sets together with a cover note saying "these two streams were combined on this date" — the history honestly shows two parallel efforts joining. Rebase is like rewriting your corrections as if you had started from the other set all along, so everything reads as one straight sequence with no cover note. Stash is like sweeping your half-finished draft forms into a labeled tray so your desk is instantly clear for an urgent task, then pulling them back out later. Cherry-pick is like spotting one specific correction in another officer's batch and copying just that single correction into your own batch.

**One line to remember:** Merge joins histories with a merge commit; rebase replays commits for a linear history; stash shelves uncommitted work; cherry-pick copies one specific commit.

sections.s2_technical:
Start with the integration problem. You have a feature branch and a main branch that have both advanced since they split. You want main's changes in your feature branch, or your feature in main. Merge and rebase are the two ways, and they differ in what the history looks like afterward.

git merge brings the branches together by creating a single new commit, the merge commit, that has two parents — the tip of your branch and the tip of the branch you merged in. Nothing is rewritten; all the original commits keep their hashes and their real timestamps, and the graph honestly shows that two lines of work diverged and then joined. The advantage is that it is non-destructive and preserves exactly what happened, which is great for shared branches and for an audit trail. The downside is that many merges produce a history with lots of merge commits and crisscrossing lines, which can be harder to read.

git rebase brings the branches together by moving the base of your branch. It sets your commits aside, fast-forwards your branch to the tip of the target, and replays your commits on top one by one, creating brand-new commits with new hashes. The result is a single straight line as if you had started from the latest target all along. The advantage is a clean, linear, easy-to-read history with no merge commits. The downside, and it is a serious one, is that it rewrites commit identities, so it must never be used on commits others have already pulled — on shared history it causes divergence and can lose work. A good rule is rebase private branches to stay current and keep history clean, but merge to integrate shared branches.

git stash solves a different problem: you are halfway through a change, your working directory is dirty, and something urgent comes up — maybe you must switch branches to fix a production bug, but Git will not let you switch cleanly with uncommitted changes that conflict. git stash takes all your uncommitted tracked changes, both staged and unstaged, saves them on a stack, and reverts your working directory to the last commit, giving you a clean tree instantly. You handle the urgent task, then run git stash pop to reapply your shelved changes and continue. You can hold multiple stashes, list them with git stash list, and apply a specific one. By default stash ignores untracked files unless you pass an include-untracked flag. It is a quick, local, temporary shelf — not a substitute for committing real work.

git cherry-pick takes exactly one commit, identified by its hash, from any branch and applies the same change as a new commit on your current branch. It does not bring the whole branch; it surgically copies a single commit. The classic use is applying one urgent fix to multiple branches — for example a hotfix commit made on a release branch that you also need on main, or a single bug fix you want to bring forward without the rest of a half-finished feature. The new commit has a different hash because its parent differs, so cherry-picking the same change into two branches creates two distinct commits. A senior-level nuance: overusing cherry-pick across long-lived branches leads to duplicated commits and confusion about where a change really originated, so it is best reserved for targeted, intentional cases like hotfix propagation. The overarching mental model is: merge and rebase are two philosophies for integrating whole branches, stash is a temporary shelf for uncommitted work, and cherry-pick is a scalpel for copying one specific commit.
sections.s3_banking:
A National Bank of India engineer is integrating a fraud-check feature, gets interrupted by a production emergency, and must also copy one specific fix across branches.

Problem 1 — the feature branch has diverged from main and the team wants to decide between a merge that preserves the branching story and a rebase that gives a clean line. This is exactly the merge-versus-rebase choice — merge for the shared integration into main, rebase for keeping the private feature branch current and tidy.

Problem 2 — midway through the fraud-check work with a dirty working directory, a production alert demands the engineer switch branches immediately. This is exactly what stash solves — shelve the half-done work, fix the emergency, then pop the work back.

Problem 3 — a single valuable fix commit exists on a release branch and is also needed on main, without dragging the rest of the release branch along. This is exactly what cherry-pick solves — copy that one commit onto main.

The mini-project is a git walkthrough covering a rebase to stay current, a merge to integrate, a stash around an interruption, and a cherry-pick of one fix. A FraudCheckService Java class is the feature so the commits map to real code.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a feature/fraud-check branch diverged from main; the engineer must stay current, get interrupted, integrate, and copy one release fix to main.

Step 1: main has advanced. The engineer rebases feature/fraud-check onto origin/main. Git replays the feature commits on top of the latest main, creating new hashes and producing a clean linear branch, keeping the private branch current without any merge commits.

Step 2: Mid-work with uncommitted edits, a production alert fires. The engineer runs git stash push, which shelves all uncommitted tracked changes onto a stack and restores a clean working tree instantly, so the engineer can switch branches without losing the half-done fraud work.

Step 3: The engineer fixes the emergency on a hotfix branch, deploys, then returns to feature/fraud-check and runs git stash pop, which reapplies the shelved changes and removes them from the stack. Work resumes exactly where it stopped.

Step 4: The feature is finished and reviewed. To integrate into the shared main, the engineer uses git merge with no-ff, creating a merge commit with two parents. Nothing is rewritten, so the history honestly records that the fraud feature was developed in parallel and merged, which is ideal for the audit trail.

Step 5: A single fix commit on release/1.5 — FRD-88, stopping false positives on international cards — is also needed on main. The engineer cherry-picks just that commit by its hash onto main, producing a new commit with the same change but a different hash.

Step 6: The engineer pushes main. The history now shows the feature merged honestly and the one release fix copied deliberately, with the stash having bridged the interruption invisibly.

```
Oct 25, 2026 04:00:02 AM INFO: rebase feature/fraud-check onto origin/main -> linear
Oct 25, 2026 04:05:11 AM WARNING: PROD alert -> git stash push "wip fraud velocity check"
Oct 25, 2026 04:20:40 AM INFO: hotfix deployed; returned to feature; git stash pop restored work
Oct 25, 2026 04:35:03 AM INFO: git merge --no-ff feature/fraud-check -> merge commit (2 parents)
Oct 25, 2026 04:40:22 AM INFO: git cherry-pick 9abc123 (FRD-88) -> new commit on main
```
sections.s5b_flow:

```
  INTEGRATION — two philosophies:

  MERGE (preserve history):             REBASE (linear history):
    o───o───M (main)                      o───o───M (main)
     \       \                                     \
      A───B───X  <- merge commit            replay: A'──B'
      (feature)   (2 parents, honest)       (feature, NEW hashes, straight)

  STASH (shelve uncommitted work):
    dirty working dir ──stash push──▶ [clean tree] ──do urgent task──▶
    ──stash pop──▶ changes restored, continue

  CHERRY-PICK (copy ONE commit):
    release/1.5:  ...─9abc123(FRD-88)─...

    main:         ...─9abc123'(new hash, same change)
```

``` ═══ LLD — merge / rebase / stash / cherry-pick ═══ ┌─ Four Operations Compared ───────────────────────────────────┐ │ merge : new merge commit, 2 parents, history preserved │ │ rebase : replay commits, new hashes, linear history │ │ stash : shelve uncommitted work on a stack (temporary) │ │ cherry-pick: copy ONE commit as a new commit on current br. │ │ Shared history? -> merge (never rebase shared) │ │ Private branch? -> rebase ok (clean + current) │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ── Commit Graph Effects ─────────────────────────────────── merge: A──B──┐ C──D──X(merge, parents B+D) rebase: A──B──C'──D' (C,D replayed onto B, new hashes) cherry-pick: X ──────► X' (single commit copied, new hash) ── State Diagram: Stash Lifecycle ───────────────────────── [dirty tree] ──stash push──→ [clean tree + stash@{0}] ▲ │ stash pop / apply └──────────────────────────────┘ (restore; pop also drops entry) │ stash drop ▼ [stash discarded] ── Command Contracts ────────────────────────────────────── git merge
Pre: on target branch Post: merge commit (2 parents) git rebase Pre: PRIVATE branch Post: linear, rewritten commits git stash push Pre: dirty tree Post: clean tree, work on stack git cherry-pick Pre: hash exists Post: new commit, same change ── Call Chain (full scenario) ───────────────────────────── 1. git rebase origin/main (private branch current + linear) 2. git stash push (interruption -> clean tree) 3. ... hotfix ... git stash pop (resume work) 4. git merge --no-ff feature (integrate into shared main) 5. git cherry-pick 9abc123 (copy release fix to main) 6. git push (publish) ```
sections.s6_takeaway:
git merge and git rebase are two ways to integrate one branch into another, and they differ in what the history looks like. Merge creates a new merge commit with two parents, joining the two lines of work. Nothing is rewritten — every original commit keeps its hash and timestamp — so the graph honestly shows that the branches diverged and then came back together. That makes merge ideal for shared branches and for an audit trail, at the cost of a busier history with many merge commits.

Rebase instead moves the base of my branch: it replays my commits one at a time on top of the latest target branch, creating brand-new commits with new hashes and producing a single straight, linear history that is much easier to read. The serious caveat is that because rebase rewrites commit identities, I must never use it on commits others have already pulled — on shared history it causes divergence and can lose work. So my rule is: rebase a private branch to stay current and keep history clean, but merge to integrate shared branches.

Stash solves a different problem. When I am halfway through a change with a dirty working directory and an urgent task forces me to switch branches, git stash takes all my uncommitted changes, saves them on a stack, and gives me a clean working tree instantly. I handle the emergency, then run git stash pop to reapply my shelved work and carry on. It is a quick temporary shelf, not a replacement for committing real work.

Cherry-pick is a scalpel. It takes exactly one commit, by its hash, from any branch and applies that same change as a new commit on my current branch. The classic use is propagating a single hotfix from a release branch to main, or bringing one bug fix forward without the rest of a half-finished feature. The copied commit gets a new hash because its parent differs. At National Bank of India I used all four on the fraud service — I rebased my private feature branch to stay linear, stashed my work when a production alert interrupted me, merged the finished feature into main with a merge commit so the history stayed honest for auditors, and cherry-picked one international-card false-positive fix from the release branch onto main. I am careful not to overuse cherry-pick, because scattering copies of the same commit across long-lived branches creates duplicates and confusion about where a change really originated.
